summary: Describes how the Type of Service field in the Internet Protocol relates to the service choices of specific networks such as AUTODIN II. It maps each network's options onto the IP precedence, delay, throughput and reliability settings. This RFC is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: Different delivery services have different speeds and prices. This memo is a translation chart between internet delivery wishes and what each network offers.

subtitle: How IP quality-of-service settings map to individual network types.

tldr.problem: The Internet Protocol defines quality-of-service fields (precedence, delay, throughput, reliability) but different networks like AUTODIN II, ARPANET, PRNET, and SATNET offer entirely different service choices with different names.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 795 provides mapping tables for each network type, showing how to translate IP Type of Service fields into each network's native service parameters.
tldr.outcome: Gateways and hosts could automatically select the closest matching network service when forwarding traffic, making multi-network systems more transparent to applications.

today: RFC 795 is Historic. The networks it describes are no longer in active use. However, the problem it addresses—mapping abstract service levels to network-specific parameters—remains relevant in modern Quality of Service and traffic engineering architectures.

sections.title: IP Type of Service Fields
sections.content: The Internet Protocol (RFC 791) includes an 8-bit Type of Service field in each packet header. Bits 0–2 specify Precedence (8 levels from Routine to Network Control). Bit 3 controls Delay (Normal or Low). Bit 4 controls Throughput (Normal or High). Bit 5 controls Reliability (Normal or High). Bits 6–7 are reserved. These fields allow hosts and routers to express quality-of-service requirements, but the meaning is abstract: actual networks support different options with different names.
sections.plainLanguage: IP packets can ask for different service levels: fast or slow, reliable or quick, important or routine. But each network underneath understands these requests differently.

sections.title: Network-Specific Mappings
sections.content: RFC 795 documents how to map IP Type of Service to four major networks. AUTODIN II distinguishes between traffic acceptance categories (Immediate/Addressed, Query/Response, and two Background levels) and application types, offering different combinations of delay, throughput, and reliability. ARPANET offers limited choices: a priority bit, message type (Type 0 regular or Type 3 uncontrolled), and message size (single packet or multipacket). PRNET (packet radio network) offers point-to-point or station routing and optional acknowledgments. SATNET (satellite network) provides the most complex options, with block vs. stream type, four delay categories, two holding-time strategies, and three reliability levels, creating 48 distinct combinations. For each network, the RFC provides tables mapping DTR (Delay-Throughput-Reliability) bit combinations to the network's native options.
sections.plainLanguage: Each network has its own buttons to press: AUTODIN has priority and application type, ARPANET has message type and size, PRNET has routing style, and SATNET has many detailed options. The tables show how to press the right buttons.

sections.title: Status and Application
sections.content: RFC 795 is a historic document reflecting the diversity of early 1980s military and research networks. Many of the networks it describes (ARPANET, PRNET, SATNET, AUTODIN II) are no longer in operation. The approach of mapping abstract service parameters to network-specific options remains sound and has evolved into modern QoS mechanisms in Internet routing protocols like DiffServ, but the specific networks and mappings in this RFC are primarily of historical interest.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is about old military and research networks from the 1980s. The idea of translating requests into what each network offers is still useful, but the specific networks have changed.

references.text: Postel, J. (ed.), "Internet Protocol - DARPA Internet Program Protocol Specification", RFC 791, ISI, September 1981.
